items.title: Palworld Card Game Teases Third Set
items.summary: The Palworld Official Card Game is giving fans a first teaser about the third set planned for the new TCG, including its official release date.
items.content:
Palworld Card Game Teases Third Set From GameRant (Written by Michael Brandon Ingram) on September 13, 2026 | OpenCritic

The Palworld Official Card Game is teasing its third set, revealing both the name of the set and the release date. The trading card game, based on mega-popular monster-catching survival game Palworld , launched its first expansion in late July.

Pocketpair and Bushiroad shocked fans in early 2026 when the companies officially revealed the upcoming Palworld Official Card Game . The collectible card game debuted on July 30 with the release of the Dawn of Palpagos set , featuring cards of fan-favorite Pals such as Daedream, Chillet, and Jormuntide. Bushiroad has already revealed some ambitious plans for the rollout of the card game as well, with the Legends Awaken expansion planned to release at the end of October, alongside the second set of Trial Decks. Now, Palworld is getting fans excited about the first set planned for 2027.

The Palworld Official Card Game is providing more details about the upcoming 2nd Edition reprints for the Dawn of Palpagos set.

Bushiroad dropped one of the first teasers for the Palworld card game's third official set on the game's social media accounts. The post revealed that the game's third set will be titled Eternal Ascent, with more information about the expansion...

items.title: Review: Palworld (PS5) - Expansive Catch 'Em All Gives Pokémon a Run for Its Money
items.content:
If ARK: Survival Evolved and Pokémon Legends Arceus had a child it’d come in the form of Palworld , a monster-taming, base-building, survival adventure title which wears it’s Pokémon inspiration proudly in the form of a medal on its breast.

Palworld has been available since September 2024 on PS5 in the form of an early access version. But it hasn’t been a smooth ride for dev Poketpair, with several lawsuits from Nintendo and The Pokemon Company against their monster-catching mechanics, specifically summoning creatures by throwing out capsules, causing delays to its development cycle.

With many months of additional work taken to fix these issues and add in hundreds of new significant features and changes, the studio has finally pushed out the 1.0 full release of its first ever open world, monster-tamer to compete with the world’s leading intellectual property, Pokémon.

The entire game is playable solo, co-op for up to four-players, or online multiplayer via a private or public server of up to 32 players. Meanwhile, the Guild system allows for friends to clan together within a server to share items and collaborate on bases without the fear of other’s disrupting or grieving their progression.

Much like other survival games, you’ll begin by customising your own character, by selecting your gender, hair style, and facial features.

You take on the role of a castaway whose ship has crash landed due to a mysterious fog and awaken on a strange beach in nothing but your underwear. You proceed with gathering sticks and rocks to craft tools and various resources to survive and thrive. After you’ve made the usual survival game tools – like an axe, spear, pickaxe and torch – you’ll progress by crafting Pal Spheres to capture Pals and level up.

In similar style to Pokémon: Legends Arceus, a vast variety of the Pals – 287 different species to be precise – can be found scattered throughout the open world environment and take little more than a toss of a Pal Sphere, a quick press of R2, to secure as a buddy. You’ll be attempting to sneak up on the vast majority since there are increased chances of capture if the Pal is struck from behind.

If you’ve played a monster-tamer before then you’ll be familiar with each creature being assigned a type which determines it’s moves, stats, and abilities. Pals are no different with a total of nine types, including Water, Grass, Fire, Ground, Electric, Ice, Dragon, Dark, and Neutral. A type advantage/disadvantage chart for battling is also available.

Types also determine which jobs they can carry out for you when roaming your base, for instance fire pals will be assigned to the furnace to smelt ore to ingots.

As with many other survival games, you’ll get as much out of Palworld as you put into it. You’re free to set out and explore the Palpagos archipelago open world as you please, with an overarching goal to search out the eight faction towers and defeat the faction bosses and their Pal companions to progress the main story.

But there's nothing stopping you from ignoring the plot entirely.

Exploring the realm should be your focus as there’s certainly no lack of activities. You’ll be traversing the terrain by climbing cliff faces, gliding across chasms and riding Pals to reach otherwise inaccessible areas.

The traversal is thrilling however sometimes you may get stuck while climbing, jitter in place, or even clip through the ground entirely, falling out of the world.

The map has a variety of areas to explore, including dungeons, beaches, ancient ruins, forests, deserts, and even a volcano.

You buy a game before it's finished, provide bug reports and feedback to developers, and help shape a project's direction and ambitions. Everybody wins: You get to play the game early, and developers earn money that helps them continue and finish their work. It's been a boon for numerous notable games over the years, including Baldur's Gate 3 and Palworld .

In an interview with GamesRadar , though, Pocketpair communications and publishing chief John Buckley said that proposition is becoming increasingly difficult for developers, because the whole idea of early access has "lost its meaning."

"Go back to the Steam Greenlight days, when Steam changed Greenlight to early access, there were a few years where it really was running and operating exactly the way I think Steam dreamed it," Buckley said.

"I think everyone knew what they were in for. The kind of people who were buying early access games knew what they were in for. They were the kind of gamers who want to be involved, they want to give feedback, they want to talk to devs. It was this really beautiful golden era."

Now, though, the rise of what Buckley called "hyper-casual mobile culture, and hyper-casual gaming culture, and live service gaming culture" has eroded that understanding, and the accord between developer and gamer that rose from it: "The culture has changed and early access, essentially, has lost its meaning. People just buy an early access game like they buy a normal game and treat it like that's the game."

Path of Exile co-creator used to think 'live service was entirely upside, in all cases', but 10 years of experience and games like Baldur's Gate 3 have shown him another way GSC Game World says there's a reason it didn't give Stalker 2 more time in the oven: 'To make something better, you need to receive feedback, and this feedback should be fresh' Palworld studio says 'gamers don't want' AI in their games: 'It feels like everyone who is super gung-ho about it isn't from the industry' There's no doubt some truth to that. Generally speaking, I subscribe to the principle that if a product is offered for sale, and people pay money for that product, they're well within their rights to expect that they're getting the product. But early access isn't quite so cut-and-dried: Steam Greenlight was a more cumbersome system, but it also clearly delineated between a work-in-progress and a final release, which early access releases often do not.

Dialed-in gamers, or those who are old enough to remember when beta testing was an actual phase of development rather than a promotional tool, may have a clearer idea of what to expect from early access games. But as gaming becomes more of a mainstream pastime it's reasonable to expect that an increasing percentage of the audience is going to neither know nor care about what early access: They just want to buy a game and play it.

From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews

Buckley doesn't believe that's necessarily a bad thing, but he did say "it's getting harder on Steam, sadly, because this culture has come through." And while he remains a believer, he also acknowledged that early access isn't ideal for every game, and that the system is "abused" by some developers.

"The biggest way it's abused now is just like, 'We'll release it now because we need money'," he said. "It's a way now to sidestep traditional funding means. It's almost become the new Kickstarter in some ways. Put out the build to get the money."

I'm not entirely sold on the idea that "put out the build to get the money" really qualifies as abuse—it is, after all, the whole basis for the early access system. But it can lead to trouble if early access sales aren't enough to support continued development, or simply through mismanaged expectations. The best thing developers who release into early access can do to avoid potential headaches, Buckley said, is to be clear about what's happening and, as much as possible, keep people fully informed.

"All we can do is try to softly educate people. I think we do an okay job. I think we try to be quite transparent. 'Hey guys, the next update's a while away. It's not going to be content-heavy, it's going to be QOL-heavy.' We try to balance it."

items.title: Palworld lead worries Steam early access has "lost its meaning": players treat it like "a normal game" and the program has been "abused for a lot of reasons"
items.content:
When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works .

(Image credit: Pocketpair) {alert('Link copied')}).catch(err => {console.error('Failed to copy: ', err)})" data-platform="copy_link" data-action="" class="font-ui-heading py-2 text-sm text-neutral-700 hover:bg-neutral-100 transition-colors no-underline block cursor-pointer border-0 bg-transparent w-full text-left normal-case" aria-label="Copy link" role="menuitem" data-analytics-id="article-social" analytics-label="utility-bar-social-share-copy-link" analytics-name="utility-bar-secondary" data-mrf-recirculation="article-social"> Copy link Facebook X Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 24 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter A shift in gaming culture has undermined Steam's early access program and stunted the perception of the games in it, worries Pocketpair and Palworld communications and publishing lead John Buckley.

Amidst Palworld's 1.0 early access graduation , Buckley discusses the work-in-progress approach with GamesRadar+. He maintains that Pocketpair is "quite confident in early access in general" and, when it comes time to make a new big thing, the studio will surely choose early access again. But that's despite what he sees as a big shift on Steam.

"Go back to the Steam Greenlight days, when Steam changed Greenlight to early access, there were a few years where it really was running and operating exactly the way I think Steam dreamed it," he says. "I think everyone knew what they were in for. The kind of people who were buying early access games knew what they were in for. They were the kind of gamers who want to be involved, they want to give feedback, they want to talk to devs. It was this really beautiful golden era."

Today, that outlook is less common, he suggests. "This continuing migration, I'll call it, of hyper-casual mobile culture, and hyper-casual gaming culture, and live service gaming culture is washing through Steam right now," Buckley notes. "Now the culture has changed and early access, essentially, has lost its meaning. People just buy an early access game like they buy a normal game and treat it like that's the game."

In Palworld's case, Buckley says players may buy the game in early access and play heavily for a week or two before arguing, "'These developers are not making new content. This game is dead.' And you're like, 'Well guys, see you in six months. We've got to make the game.'"

People don't understand Steam player numbers, Palworld lead says: "Poor Marathon" Pocketpair lead thought if Palworld 1.0 hit 200k players, "that'd be party time" – it passed 900k The game Palworld dev Pocketpair "would not exist without" is ready to escape Early Access prison

Buckley clarifies that he doesn't think "it's a bad thing that some gamers aren't interested" in how the sausage is made, even if quietly raising "the general knowledge level around game development" might help both sides. "You just want to enjoy a nice thing, and that's fair enough. No shade there." (In 2025, we spoke to dozens of game devs about things players get wrong about how games are made .)

Nonetheless, he says, "It's getting harder on Steam, sadly, because this culture has come through. I think consoles are where it struggles the most because console gamers aren't used to the concept of early access gameplay. Again, that's fine. You get less feedback from those players in general versus PC gamers, who love to drown you in bug reports. Look, all we can do is try to softly educate people. I think we do an okay job. I think we try to be quite transparent. 'Hey guys, the next update's a while away. It's not going to be content-heavy, it's going to be QOL-heavy.' We try to balance it."

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

Recently, Buckley has been shaping expectations for update 1.1 , reiterating that Palworld will continue but is not due for another massive overhaul. Earlier in the year, he said he "wouldn't rule out a Palworld 2.0 ," but fans also shouldn't expect a No Man's Sky-style arrangement with 10 years of heavy support. (As it happens, we spoke to No Man's Sky boss Sean Murray about 10 years of support.)

Though Pocketpair has chosen early access multiple times and remain "big advocates" for it – Craftopia, its previous survival game, is approaching its own 1.0 update – Buckley agrees it's not right for every project.

"There are many real cases of early access just being a disaster for some games," he says. "I think it just depends on how receptive you want to be. Early access has now been abused for a lot of reasons. The biggest way it's abused now is just like, 'We'll release it now because we need money.' It's a way now to sidestep traditional funding means. It's almost become the new Kickstarter in some ways. Put out the build to get the money. But we're big fans of it."

Splashing some of its Palworld cash, Pocketpair's publishing arm has, like many other newly formed devs-turned-publishers, sought to find and fund promising games at a time of dire investment opportunities in the games industry.

items.title: Now Available on TCGplayer: Palworld Official Card Game and Cyberpunk TCG
items.summary: We are excited to announce full support for all currently available products for Palworld Official Card Game and Cyberpunk TCG.
items.content:
Return to Seller Blog Post Tags #new TCG , #new product lines , #New Game , #bushiroad , #Palworld , #Cyberpunk TCG , #Palworld Official Card Game Now Available on TCGplayer: Palworld Official Card Game and Cyberpunk TCG By Janice Rivera-Pagan • August 31, 2026 It’s a two-title launch: Palworld Official Card Game and Cyberpunk TCG are now available to list on the TCGplayer Marketplace!

The newest card game to debut from the publisher Bushiroad ( Cardfight Vanguard, Weiss Schwarz, etc.), Palworld Official Card Game reached explosive levels of popularity nearly overnight after its launch on July 30 of this year.

At the same time, Cyberpunk TCG is an up-and-coming card game slated to release November, but Kickstarter backers will be receiving some highly-anticipated, exclusive “preem” product in early September.

We are excited to announce full support for all currently available products for Palworld Official Card Game and Cyberpunk TCG. This includes sealed and singles for the first Palworld booster set, “Dawn of Palpagos” as well as the first two Trial Decks and any exclusive promotional cards. As for Cyberpunk TCG, all the products from the Kickstarter campaign (such as the booster box, the pre-built starter decks, and the Kickstarter exclusive cards) will also be available.

Sellers are now able to list their inventory for both Palworld Official Card Game and Cyberpunk TCG prior to the games’ launch on the TCGplayer Marketplace.

For more information on these card games, please visit the Palworld Official Card Game and Cyberpunk TCG official websites.

Have questions or feedback for our team? Contact us at catalog@tcgplayer.com .

items.content:
\

Palworld version v1.0.3 has been released!

＝＝＝

\

▼Items and Equipment ・Changed the unlock level of some Jetragon-related technologies from 79 to 70, and reduced the materials required for the Pal Gear used to ride Jetragon.

・Changed the technology unlock level of the Aquatic Construction Kit from Level 66 to Level 23, changed its Ancient Technology Point requirement from 4 to 1, and adjusted the required materials and work amount.

・Extended the duration of World Tree Holy Water.

・Reduced the weight of World Tree Holy Water from 1 to 0.1.

・Added World Tree Holy Water to the rewards for World Tree expeditions, World Tree fishing, and the Large Fishing Pond.

・Increased the amount of World Tree Holy Water obtained from Pals in The World Tree area.

・Increased the amount of World Tree Holy Water obtained from Teafant Spring.

・Adjusted the work amount required to craft the Ancient Armor series.

・Doubled the amount of Fiber obtained from trees.

▼Bases and Missions

・Reduced the building costs of the Crude Oil Extractor, High-Pressure Crude Oil Extractor, and Large Power Generator.

・Increased the crude oil production speed of the Crude Oil Extractor and High-Pressure Crude Oil Extractor.

・The base mission that requires building a Crude Oil Extractor can now also be progressed by building a High-Pressure Crude Oil Extractor.

▼Server Settings

・Added a server setting (bAllowEnemyCampSpawnNearBaseCamp) that disables the suppression of enemy camp spawns near player base camps.

\

▼Graphics and Display

・Adjusted the boundary display in some areas to make it easier to see from a distance.

・Improved the display quality of some objects in dungeons.

▼Sound

・Added a sound effect when using World Tree Holy Water.

\

▼Crashes and Progression Blockers

・Fixed an issue where the mission could become impossible to progress if the barrier was removed before accepting the main mission in Sunreach.

▼Multiplayer and Co-op

・Fixed an issue in co-op where lighting on the client side could display incorrectly after cutscenes or the ending played.

・Fixed an issue in co-op where some scenes could stutter during the cutscene that plays when entering The World Tree.

・Fixed an issue on dedicated servers where Fast Travel could activate unintentionally during Tower Boss battles.

・Fixed an issue on dedicated servers where Pals could appear to vibrate rapidly on the client screen.

▼Pals and NPCs

・Fixed an issue where the summoned Pal could stop fighting.

items.title: This New Survival Game Finally Clicked with Me, and I'm Never Looking Back
items.summary: Palworld 1.0 does a great job of easing you into its many complex systems.
items.content:
Survival games have been wildly popular for years now. I’ve dabbled here and there to see what the fuss is about, but I’ve always fallen off after a few hours. Usually, I get tangled up in one meagerly explained system after another until I lose track of what I’m supposed to do, and my time with the game peters out.

When Palworld 1.0 came out to rave reviews , I figured I’d give the genre another shot – and I’m glad I did. Palworld’s gradual, newbie-friendly onboarding helped me see what a whole lot of people have loved about survival games all along. Palworld made me a believer.

I’m glad I came in at the 1.0 mark, because I’ve heard Palworld had a much steeper learning curve out of the gate. But now, new players start with a series of missions designed to guide you through the game’s numerous systems . You learn how to punch trees to get wood to create a crafting bench. You learn how to make a club you can use to beat some Pals to death (it’s a dog-eat-dog world out there) to get wool. You then use that wool to make clothes. You set up a camp. You build a house. You activate a teleporter and explore deeper into the game world.

Before long, you’re gliding off cliffs Zelda-style before whomping on every Pal you see to catch them in spheres to put them to work. You can deploy them at your camp, ride them , or have them fight by your side to take on big roaming Pals and towering bosses . It’s a blast. And there’s no way I would have stuck with it if it hadn’t held my hand and eased me into the systems that make up the game.

I still have a long way to go, because I was nowhere near powerful enough to defeat the first boss solo. But those early missions gave me a much-needed handle on what else I can spend my time doing as I level up enough to become a threat. There's a vast world out there I can keep exploring, all while catching Pals and building up my base. I’m having a blast doing it.

Palworld’s 1.0 is available on Steam , Xbox , and PS5 . It costs $29.99, but you can save a few bucks on a Steam copy at Fanatical , which is currently running its summer sale .

Chris Reed is a commerce editor and deals expert for IGN. He also runs IGN's board game and LEGO coverage. You can follow him on Bluesky .

} .login #login, .login #lostpasswordform { min-width: 350px !important; } .wpforms-field-c4wp iframe { width: 100% !important; } ","library":"fa-solid"},"toggle":"burger"}" data-widget_type="nav-menu.default"> CBB CFB MLB NBA NFL Sports Media More Auto Racing Gambling Golf Lists MMA NHL Tennis Video Games Watch World Cup WNBA WWE CBB CFB MLB NBA NFL Sports Media More Auto Racing Gambling Golf Lists MMA NHL Tennis Video Games Watch World Cup WNBA WWE ","library":"fa-solid"},"toggle":"burger"}" data-widget_type="nav-menu.default"> CBB CFB MLB NBA NFL Sports Media More Auto Racing Gambling Golf Lists MMA NHL Tennis Video Games Watch World Cup WNBA WWE CBB CFB MLB NBA NFL Sports Media More Auto Racing Gambling Golf Lists MMA NHL Tennis Video Games Watch World Cup WNBA WWE Facebook Twitter Instagram Youtube Linkedin Palworld review: Fresh and innovative, despite appearances By Ryan Woodrow | July 22, 2026 Photo Credit: Pocketpair When Palworld first launched into early access two and a half years ago, I described it as a “breath of fresh air” for the survival-crafting genre, and in the time since then, the state of that genre hasn’t changed. I still find it to be one of the most stagnant genres out there, with a formula that I once found enjoyable when Minecraft and Terraria stumbled upon it, but has now been worn into the ground by every early access game on Steam.

That’s why I was so surprised how much creature collecting adds to that formula, but now the game has hit 1.0 and officially launched, I can see it goes a lot deeper than just slapping a couple hundred colorful creatures on top of the standard survival-crafting affair.

The Pals that roam the world aren’t just set dressing or collectibles; they’re integral to every single part of the core loop. Upon defeating or catching them, you get resources vital to progression that can’t be obtained through any other means; catching them is your main source of EXP, which is how you progress through the game’s tech tree; and most importantly, you can put the Pals to work at your base to complete tasks for you.

While the trailers for the game present this as a funny, edgy thing where they’re emphasizing the darker elements of the world that Pokémon likes to gloss over, putting Pals to work is a vital part of the game, and a surprisingly deep system.

There are 12 different work suitabilities that determine what tasks a Pal can perform. This includes things like planting, crafting, smelting, watering, and a bunch more, and each one has levels from 0 to 10 showing how quickly they’ll perform the task. This means that, as your base grows, finding the right balance of Pal proficiencies is vital to making meaningful progress, especially as, once you get out of the early game, there are many things that you won’t be able to do yourself.

Source: Pocketpair Take smelting, for example. You can’t just slap some coal in a furnace and wait for everything to cook; you have to get a fire Pal to cook it for you, and as you go up each tier of material, you’re going to need to find Pals that are much better at that task to get it done in a reasonable time frame.

And that’s all without taking into account the passive and partner skill systems, where every species of Pal has a unique partner skill, and every single Pal you catch has a random selection of passives that either help or hinder their work. It makes you actually care deeply about your Pals, as you’re paying attention to their every detail. While in Pokémon, you only have to worry about breeding and traits if you want to play competitively, in Palworld, that stuff is baked into the foundation of the singleplayer experience.

Not to mention, it also helps build the world, the lore, and the characters of the Pals. While some partner skills will be passive boosts, there are some Pal duos, like Anubis and Sehkmet, that specifically boost each other when working together, giving you another layer of considerations to make when organizing your base.

If that all sounds complicated, it really isn’t, as the game makes it very easy to manage. Early on, you’ll unlock a podium that lets you assign Pals to specific tasks, as well as dictate which of their proficiencies they are and aren’t allowed to use when unassigned, to ensure that everyone focuses on the jobs you intend for them.

But all of these Pals don’t just wander in unannounced; you have to seek them out in the world, which is Palworld’s other great strength: the exploration.

With an impressive draw distance, as soon as you walk out into the world, you’ll spot all kinds of wondrous sights. Volcanoes, snow mountains, lush forests, and even oil rigs all litter the landscape, and if you can see it, you can go there. The only restriction is the World Tree, which is locked behind endgame progression, but even that makes for a tantalizing mystery constantly on the horizon that you’re working towards.

Source: Pocketpair You settle into a well-paced loop where you work improving your base for a while, which in turn improves your gear so you can then go and explore further afield into higher-level areas with brand new Pals to catch, boosting your EXP and giving you new resources to help you progress even further when you return to base. It’s a simple loop, but one that so many survival-crafting games fail to implement satisfyingly; that’s the power of a creature collector.

So let’s talk about the Pals themselves, because with 204 unique designs and 278 total designs when you include hybrids – which are elemental variants on existing Pals that only vary in color – there are honestly very few misses among the pack. There are a handful of basic ones you probably won’t give much thought to, but the vast majority of Pals have a tangible charisma to their designs that makes them compelling.

I actually found the game’s five-Pal party quite restrictive considering how many cool designs there were that I wanted to use on my team, though this is where having many slots at your base for workers helps, as you do form relationships with those Pals too.
